entries.note: This reports his private concerns and their intensity.
The accusation concerns deliberate fabrication and investors' private motives; missing the projected figures would not establish those motives.
The asserted exclusive purpose of the paragraph is a claim about intent.
'I cannot see a viable (or reasonable) path' expresses doubt rather than a firm prediction that an IPO will not happen.

entries.test: Comparative financial disclosures and spending on video, browser and speaker projects would show whether avoiding those projects materially improved Anthropic's financial condition relative to OpenAI.
entries.note: The financial context supplies a plain reading of 'better condition'; the sentence also explicitly attributes a cause.
The main claim judges the usefulness of a financial metric. The subsidiary assertion about token revenue could be checked separately.

entries.test: Dated revenue reports would establish OpenAI's seven-month progression toward $40 billion annualized revenue and Anthropic's reported May and July run rates.
entries.note: The source elsewhere gives a conflicting month for Anthropic's $65 billion figure; that does not make this extraction unfaithful.
This sentence gives an overarching judgment without identifying which commitments are literally impossible.

entries.test: An OpenAI IPO and the companies' contemporaneous financial disclosures would establish whether OpenAI could go public without competitive revenues and losses.
entries.note: This asserts a necessary condition for an IPO; the growth and customer-base comparisons are separately checkable present facts.
'Anything in modern history' is sweeping hyperbole without a defined comparable quantity.

entries.test: Anthropic's disclosed contracts and financial results would establish commitments exceeding $300 billion due within three years of publication and its losses relative to OpenAI's.
entries.note: The claim concerns existing obligations, even though their payment dates are future.

entries.test: Financial and financing disclosures following accelerated OpenAI revenue growth would show whether costs also accelerated and several additional $122 billion funding rounds became necessary.
entries.note: The predicted financing consequence is conditional on revenue acceleration.

entries.test: Successive annual cash requirements and funding disclosures would show whether OpenAI needed more than its preceding funding request every year.
entries.note: A year in which it demonstrably needed no increase would contradict the categorical claim.
The preceding list supports the two-outcome extraction. 'Largest and most-successful company of all time' has no shared measure.

entries.test: Public reporting on private-credit fundraising attempts for data centers and OpenAI would show whether difficulty funding the former coincided with substantial difficulty attracting investors to the latter.
entries.note: Failed, delayed or materially reduced fundraising efforts supply a plain practical test.

entries.test: Funding-round disclosures separating venture-capital contributions from corporate and other investors would show whether either company raised more than $30 billion of venture capital in one round.
entries.note: The context limits the ceiling to venture capital; the normalized proposition states an unrestricted fundraising ceiling.
'Show' strengthens the source's 'suggests.' The liquidation premise is explicitly framed as very unlikely.

entries.test: Public insolvency records and financial reporting would establish whether OpenAI collapsed when a major payment became due and further financing was unavailable.
entries.note: The uncertainty concerns when, while the predicted collapse mechanism is firm.

entries.test: OpenAI's Q1 2026 cash-flow reconciliation would show whether capital inflows alone accounted for its improved cash position.
entries.note: 'Only by virtue of' expressly attributes the improvement to a cause.

entries.test: Cash balances, payment obligations and financing disclosures through November 18, 2026 would show whether OpenAI needed additional money within three months of publication.
entries.note: The need for money is firm; its amount and the predicted upfront payments are hedged.

entries.test: Financial disclosures, unit-cost trends, pricing changes and enterprise customer responses would show whether rising service costs and pricing constraints caused OpenAI's continuing financing needs.
entries.note: The enterprise example supports the extracted causal claim rather than adding a condition.

entries.test: Revenue-growth reports for both companies and evidence of corporate token-maxxing spending through December 31, 2026 would establish the predicted slowdown and year-end petering out of those initiatives.
entries.note: The explicit year-end deadline applies to token-maxxing initiatives; the broader slowdown has no separate deadline.

entries.test: Ramp's published adoption findings and evidence of customer responses to model price increases would test the claimed price barrier.
entries.note: The normalization explicitly extends the Fable-based conclusion to both companies, beyond the sentence's stated scope.

entries.test: Public investor questions and OpenAI responses following an Anthropic September IPO would show whether OpenAI had to defend both companies' economics.
entries.note: The IPO is the antecedent; the predicted defensive response has no stated deadline.

entries.test: An announced or completed subsequent OpenAI fundraising round would establish the firmly expected fundraising event.
entries.note: 'Expect' is firm; asset-manager predominance and NVIDIA participation remain probabilistic qualifications.
The forecast concerns Altman's private consideration of an IPO. The judgment that an IPO is terrible is also evaluative.
The composite assessment of a 'desperate and untenable' position and an unclear escape has no agreed settling test.

entries.test: If Microsoft absorbed OpenAI, its initial contract actions and revised Azure guidance would show whether it canceled effectively all cloud contracts and removed $250 billion of incremental spend.
entries.note: A hypothetical future acquisition is a testable antecedent, not an inherently untestable counterfactual.
Both product changes are expressly qualified by 'potentially' or 'likely.'
He presents this outcome as something that 'could' happen.

entries.test: Comparative financial results and Anthropic's contractual obligations, resources and subsequent fulfillment would establish its unprofitability and ability to keep the commitments.
entries.note: The current-loss comparison is already assessable; definitive fulfillment or failure can settle the asserted inability to meet promises.

entries.test: OpenAI's revenue, obligation payments and continued viability through August 18, 2029 would test whether the specified financial achievements were necessary to defeat Zitron's collapse thesis.
entries.note: The normalization omits the explicit 27% comparison with three companies' combined revenues. The source also mixes a three-year horizon with 2030 projections.
The surrounding sentences supply the OpenAI-collapse condition, but SoftBank's death is only a possibility.
This asserts an elevated likelihood, not a firm outcome.

entries.test: Following an OpenAI collapse, public records of unpaid obligations, counterparty losses and investment write-downs would establish whether economic damage occurred.
entries.note: The preceding discussion supplies a concrete financial meaning for 'damage.'

entries.test: Compute contracts, equity-funding flows, independent customer demand and industry investment disclosures would test whether circularly funded capacity purchases produced a misleading appearance of AI demand.
entries.note: The normalization weakens 'the entire industry' and 'every ounce of compute capacity,' and drops the explicit motive attribution. The central demand-and-financing mechanism has a public evidentiary test.
